heading|1||About this catalogue|0|1|preliminar|3|2|lead=This catalogue gathers fourteen Spanish paintings: thirteen held by three American museums that have released their collections under a CC0 licence, the Metropolitan Museum in New York, the National Gallery in Washington and the Cleveland Museum of Art, and one from the Museo Sorolla in Madrid reproduced from the public-domain Google Art Project scan.;style=preliminar||:About this catalogue||||

part|0|I|El Greco|1|1||1|4||band=#3d4a63|||||
heading|1|1|View of Toledo|1|1||2|5|cat=1;catlabel=Cat.;lead=View of Toledo, is one of the two surviving landscapes painted by El Greco, along with View and Plan of Toledo. View of Toledo is held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City.;tombstone=ca. 1599–1600 · Oil on canvas · 121.3 × 108.6 cm · The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York · 29.100.6||:View of Toledo||||
heading|1|2|Cardinal Fernando Niño de Guevara|1|1||4|7|cat=2;catlabel=Cat.;lead=Portrait of Fernando Niño de Guevara is a 1600 painting of cardinal Fernando Niño de Guevara by El Greco, now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.;tombstone=ca. 1600 · Oil on canvas · 170.8 × 108 cm · The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York · 29.100.5||:Cardinal Fernando Niño de Guevara||||
heading|1|3|Laocoön|1|1||6|9|cat=3;catlabel=Cat.;lead=The Laocoön is an oil painting created between 1610 and 1614 by Greek painter El Greco. It is part of a collection at the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C.;tombstone=c. 1610–1614 · Oil on canvas · 137.5 × 172.5 cm · National Gallery of Art, Washington · 1946.18.1||:Laocoön||||
part|0|II|Jusepe de Ribera|1|1||9|12||band=#4a3b32|||||
heading|1|4|The Tears of Saint Peter|1|1||10|13|cat=4;catlabel=Cat.;lead=Saint Peter has just denied Christ three times and weeps. Ribera paints him half length, hands clasped and reddened eyes turned upwards; beside him the keys of heaven rest on the rock. The dark ground and the raw light falling on brow and hands come straight from Caravaggio.;tombstone=ca. 1612–1613 · Oil on canvas · 161.9 × 114.3 cm · The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York · 2012.416||:The Tears of Saint Peter||||
part|0|III|Diego Velázquez|1|1||13|16||band=#6e3535|||||
heading|1|5|Juan de Pareja|1|1||14|17|cat=5;catlabel=Cat.;lead=The Portrait of Juan de Pareja is a painting by Spanish artist Diego Velázquez of the enslaved Juan de Pareja, a notable painter in his own right, who was owned by Velázquez at the time the painting was completed. Velázquez painted the portrait in Rome, while traveling in Italy, in 1650.;tombstone=1650 · Oil on canvas · 81.3 × 69.9 cm · The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York · 1971.86||:Juan de Pareja||||
heading|1|6|The Needlewoman|1|1||16|19|cat=6;catlabel=Cat.;lead=The Needlewoman is an oil-on-canvas painting by Diego Velázquez, painted between 1635 and 1643. It is housed in the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C.;tombstone=c. 1640–1650 · Oil on canvas · 74 × 60 cm · National Gallery of Art, Washington · 1937.1.81||:The Needlewoman||||
part|0|IV|Francisco de Zurbarán|1|1||19|22||band=#55534d|||||
heading|1|7|Saint Lucy|1|1||20|23|cat=7;catlabel=Cat.;lead=Saint Lucy steps towards us dressed like a Sevillian lady on a feast day: gold brocade, a red mantle, a lace collar. Only two objects give away the martyr of Syracuse: the palm she holds in one hand and, in the other, the dish with the two eyes that, according to legend, were torn from her and made her the patron saint of sight.;tombstone=c. 1625–1630 · Oil on canvas · 104.1 × 77 cm · National Gallery of Art, Washington · 1943.7.11||:Saint Lucy||||
heading|1|8|Christ and the Virgin in the House at Nazareth|1|1||22|25|cat=8;catlabel=Cat.;lead=In a dim room the boy Christ is weaving a crown of thorns and has just pricked his finger. Across from him the Virgin has let her sewing fall into her lap and weeps in silence: she understands what that drop of blood foretells. No one else witnesses the scene but two doves and a light that falls diagonally from above.;tombstone=c. 1640 · Oil on canvas · 165 × 218.2 cm · Cleveland Museum of Art · 1960.117||:Christ and the Virgin in the House at Nazareth||||
part|0|V|Bartolomé Esteban Murillo|1|1||25|28||band=#8a6a3b|||||
heading|1|9|Two Women at a Window|1|1||26|29|cat=9;catlabel=Cat.;lead=Two women look out of a window: a girl leans on the sill and smiles at someone in the street, while an older woman, half hidden by the shutter, covers her laugh with her veil. The window frame is the frame of the picture, and the joke, whatever it is, is shared with the viewer.;tombstone=c. 1655–1660 · Oil on canvas · 125.1 × 104.5 cm · National Gallery of Art, Washington · 1942.9.46||:Two Women at a Window||||
heading|1|10|Virgin and Child|1|1||28|31|cat=10;catlabel=Cat.;lead=Seated on a stone bench, the Virgin steadies the Child standing on her lap as he turns towards the viewer. There is no throne, no angels, no crown: only a young mother with an Andalusian face, a white cloth and a background of clouds that opens into light behind the figures.;tombstone=1670s · Oil on canvas · 165.7 × 109.2 cm · The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York · 43.13||:Virgin and Child||||
part|0|VI|Francisco Goya|1|1||31|34||band=#5f6b5a|||||
heading|1|11|Manuel Osorio Manrique de Zuñiga|1|1||32|35|cat=11;catlabel=Cat.;lead=Manuel Osorio Manrique de Zúñiga is a large full-length portrait in oil painted in 1787–88 by the Spanish artist Francisco Goya. It depicts a boy three or four years of age, standing in red clothes, with birds and cats. It is also known as Goya's ”Red Boy”.;tombstone=1787–1788 · Oil on canvas · 127 × 101.6 cm · The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York · 49.7.41||:Manuel Osorio Manrique de Zuñiga||||
heading|1|12|The Marquesa de Pontejos|1|1||34|37|cat=12;catlabel=Cat.;lead=María Ana de Pontejos y Sandoval, Marquesa de Pontejos, was painted by Goya around 1786, the year of her marriage to the brother of the Count of Floridablanca, the king's first minister. She stands full length in a garden, in a pale silk dress of the latest French fashion, a carnation in her hand and a pug at her feet.;tombstone=c. 1786 · Oil on canvas · 210.3 × 127 cm · National Gallery of Art, Washington · 1937.1.85||:The Marquesa de Pontejos||||
heading|1|13|Señora Sabasa García|1|1||36|39|cat=13;catlabel=Cat.;lead=María García Pérez de Castro, known as Sabasa García, was barely in her twenties when Goya painted her. Tradition has it that the painter saw her at the house of her uncle, the minister Evaristo Pérez de Castro, while working on his portrait, and asked to paint her on the spot.;tombstone=c. 1806–1811 · Oil on canvas · 71 × 58 cm · National Gallery of Art, Washington · 1937.1.88||:Señora Sabasa García||||

heading|1|14|Strolling along the Seashore|1|1||40|43|cat=14;catlabel=Cat.;lead=It has a height of 205 cm and a width of 200 cm. and shows the wife and eldest daughter of the painter during a walk on the beach in Valencia. The painting is part of the collection of the Museo Sorolla in Madrid.;tombstone=1909 · Oil on canvas · 205 × 200 cm · Museo Sorolla, Madrid||:Strolling along the Seashore||||
